name: Erik Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, 43, and I lead the awkward electrical repairs in homes and businesses. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the firm's strongest practical electricians, earning above the usual rate. My partner repairs upholstery; we have children aged eight and thirteen, a mortgage and fifteen months of expenses saved, with plenty of electrical employers nearby. I use AI daily for checked notes and parts descriptions, and we've been considering a larger house partly because I'd like room for a workbench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a tool can earn a place without earning a headline. I use AI every day to organise checked notes and compare parts descriptions. I'd rather have the crew home on time than find another word for how modern the job sheet looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages cover the mortgage and family costs, and we've got fifteen months of expenses saved. My pay is higher than usual, and there are plenty of electrical employers nearby. My partner repairs upholstery, so a mild change in thinking tools doesn't make me expect either income to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the difficult home and business repairs and checking the finished work. Starting now I'd continue matching every drafted note to my actual readings. Through the first year we'd keep our ordinary household budget, including looking carefully at the larger house we'd already been considering, rather than buy something because a forecast sounded reassuring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own living. I like a useful improvement, but I don't need one to pay the next bill. A strong reserve means I can say no to a clever idea and still be interested in the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you the person leading the difficult work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the strongest practical electricians at the firm. I get the faults that need patient tracing and make sure the crew understand the final checks. Daily AI use doesn't make me willing to hand over that responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is behind the larger-house idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I have children aged eight and thirteen, and we'd like more space, but I'd also like a room for my workbench. A bigger house would give my tools more space, not just the children. We haven't signed anything, and the present house works; it just doesn't fit every project I imagine.

say: I'd keep a **useful tool** without needing a headline about it.
I'd value the **crew getting home** more than a fashionable description of the job sheet.
think: Our **current wages** cover costs, with fifteen months saved, higher pay and plentiful local electrical employers.
My partner's **upholstery repairs** also look secure in this mild picture, so our own living feels comfortable.
do: Keep **leading difficult repairs** and checking finished crew work through the first year.
Continue checking daily **AI drafts** against readings while keeping the ordinary family budget and uncommitted house search.
feel: **Calm** about work and household money, with enough reserve to reject an idea without fearing the next bill.
S0.quote: A bigger house would give my tools more space, not just the children.
fieldNote: His **security** is grounded in higher pay, fifteen months saved, two physical jobs and many local employers rather than assumed machine-proof skill.
He admits the **house upgrade** partly serves his own hobby, while no contract or payment commitment has yet been made.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and checking daily drafts against actual readings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's automate a small boring step and count what still needs checking. I'd offer to set up the approved AI invoice drafter after the owner agreed a paid test. I'd want the office seeing the mistakes, not just my best example.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own pay to stay steady over the next few years because the repair work is there and most of it still needs hands. My partner's upholstery work is physical too. I don't think using a tool early protects every job forever, but this picture looks useful for our household rather than frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a two-week invoice-draft trial only with owner approval, all work paid and normal weekly wages and hours unchanged. I'd use completed jobs first, with the office checking amounts and approving anything before a customer received it. During the first year I'd keep leading repairs and stop the drafter if it invented work, prices or test results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and keen to see the result. I like an experiment with a clear limit and somebody allowed to point out what I missed. Being first to suggest a tool shouldn't mean being last to admit it failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the AI send the invoice itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the office would check the actual agreed work and amounts before authorising anything to go out. An AI invoice draft can save typing without deciding what the customer owes. I'd stop the trial if it invented an item rather than quietly tidy the example for a presentation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would pay for setup time or a new subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The employer, with approval before spending and the work inside paid hours. I'd wait if normal weekly wages and hours couldn't be kept. I'm offering a trial, not a free evening or a household account for the firm's software.

say: I'd automate a **small boring step** while counting the checks still needed.
I'd show the **office mistakes** as openly as the best example from a trial.
think: My **near-term pay** looks steady while physical repair demand continues.
Both **physical jobs** look secure here, without implying early tool use guarantees permanent safety.
do: Trial **AI invoices** two weeks only with owner approval, employer-paid setup and subscriptions, paid time and normal wages and hours retained.
Use **completed jobs** first and require office checks and approval before anything reaches a customer.
Keep **repair leadership** and stop the drafter for invented work, prices or readings.
feel: **Calm** about current livelihoods, with enthusiasm for a bounded test that can honestly fail.
S1.quote: An AI invoice draft can save typing without deciding what the customer owes.
fieldNote: The **automation** is a new invoice-drafting function, not routine daily notes relabelled as learning or autonomous billing without approval.
His **paid trial** retains employer costs, owner permission, normal wages and hours, completed-job testing and human authorisation before customer use.

steps.text: Trial AI invoices two weeks only with owner approval and employer-funded setup and subscriptions
Set up only inside paid hours with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged
Use completed jobs first; require office approval before sending invoices; stop invented work, prices or readings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI arrives in 2028 and capable robots around 2031, so a trade isn't an exemption from the whole picture. I'd still use the thinking tools where they helped, with the proper checks. I'd tell the family we could make a choice without pretending the future had already sent us an invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could shrink when robots compete for the ordinary installation work behind our repair diary. My partner's upholstery income could face the same physical competition. Fifteen months saved gives us room to judge actual offers and prices, not a guarantee that we could rebuild both incomes on demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my partner to agree that we stop the larger-house search now and keep the present mortgage plan. We hadn't signed anything, so there would be no refund to invent or extra cash to call new saving. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep actual paid repairs, reviewing both wages monthly and making no new housing commitment without agreement and real costs in front of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about later household earnings, with enough resources to slow a decision down. I can want a bigger workshop and still decide the family doesn't need that risk today. I'd rather be honest about what the extra room was for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your partner have to accept the paused search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd discuss it and agree before changing the shared plan. I'd explain the work risk and the costs I wanted to check, not announce that my nerves had become the household rule. A house plan needs both adults, not just the person drawing a workbench in the spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a different employer automatically solve the robot risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd compare an actual offer if one existed, but I haven't chosen an application campaign from this card. I'd ask about paid hours, wages and travel before making any decision. Plenty of firms now isn't a promise that all of them keep hiring later.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking AI** from robots around 2031 without declaring a trade permanently sheltered.
I'd use **checked tools** while making family choices from actual risks rather than treating a forecast as a bill.
think: Both **household repair incomes** could shrink when capable robots compete for physical work.
Our **fifteen-month reserve** gives decision time, not guaranteed replacement earnings from every nearby employer.
do: Pause the **larger-house search** now only by agreement with my partner, keeping the existing mortgage plan.
Budget from **actual wages**, counting no refund or new saving from a house contract we never signed.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and review both wages monthly before any agreed housing commitment.
feel: **Anxious** about later household earnings, with enough resources to postpone a personally attractive risk.
S2.quote: I can want a bigger workshop and still decide the family doesn't need that risk today.
fieldNote: The **housing pause** changes an existing plan only with partner agreement, creating neither a refund nor new saving from retained cash.
His **employer comparisons** remain comparisons, while possible physical-income loss supports anxiety with control rather than an asserted catastrophic outcome.

steps.text: Pause larger-house search only with partner agreement, keeping the existing mortgage plan
Keep paid repairs after 2028 and review actual household wages monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us check the family plan twice instead of make one decision out of fear. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and robots around 2034, so I wouldn't call the physical work safe forever. I'd still want to enjoy some of the years we were given.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our current physical wages to hold over the next few years, with a strong reserve and plenty of local firms. I'd be 48 in 2031, and the children would be thirteen and eighteen, so the family would still need an income. I'm uneasy about later competition without expecting a wage crisis next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the house search for eighteen months by agreement with my partner, then review actual figures rather than restart automatically. We'd resume searching only with continuing agreement, the fifteen-month reserve untouched and written wages covering moving fees, new housing and travel costs. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep actual paid repairs and repeat that check before any move commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later market, but able to give a family choice its proper size. I don't want to forbid a larger house forever because a machine date frightens me. I don't want a workbench wish quietly eating the emergency account either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the eighteen-month review include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real asking prices, all moving fees, the new monthly housing payment and travel, compared with our actual written wages. We'd keep the full reserve outside the purchase money. If either adult didn't agree or the numbers failed, the search would wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would restarting a search mean you had bought the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd still need to see real terms before any commitment. Looking at a house listing isn't a payment plan. I'd keep a wish and a signed cost on different pages until the decision was real.

say: I'd use **five years** for checked decisions without declaring either permanent danger or permanent safety.
I'd keep **family enjoyment** inside preparation rather than treat every comfortable choice as a failure to plan.
think: Our **near-term physical wages** look steady with a strong reserve and plenty of local firms.
At **48**, I'd still need household earnings, while later robot competition remains unresolved.
do: Pause the **house search** for eighteen months only with partner agreement, then review rather than restart automatically.
Resume only with **continuing agreement**, the reserve untouched and written wages covering moving fees, new housing and travel.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and repeat the affordability check before any move commitment.
feel: **Uneasy** about later competition, with room to reconsider a wanted house without risking the emergency reserve.
S3.quote: Looking at a house listing isn't a payment plan.
fieldNote: His **household review** has a date and continuing consent rather than a promised purchase, with fees, housing and travel included.
The **reserve boundary** remains intact, and near-term confidence does not become assumed retirement or a physical specialism beyond the later robots.

steps.text: Pause house search eighteen months with partner agreement; restart only with consent and reserve untouched
Resume only when written wages cover all moving fees, new housing and travel costs
Keep actual paid repairs after 2031 and recheck costs before a move commitment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to choose what we actually want, not only react to what we fear. I'd keep paid work and useful experiments, but I wouldn't make the children join my trade to prove the family was ready. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 still arrive while I expect to need earnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when robots followed, so I can't assume a pension settles the mortgage. Our current wages and fifteen-month reserve make the next few years secure. I can enjoy that while admitting the jobs, the house balance and the children's later support needs are not all known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present house for a year by agreement with my partner, then review actual prices and wages. We'd resume searching only with continuing agreement, the reserve untouched and written wages covering moving fees, new housing and travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep actual paid repairs and make no house commitment before repeating the full household check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, with no need to promise myself the same job forever. I'd like the children to remember a father who built things and came home, not somebody always practising being frightened. A reserve should give us time to think and some permission to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the older children automatically make a move simpler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be eighteen and twenty-three in 2036, but I don't know where they'd live or what help they'd need. We'd ask and use the actual circumstances then. Their possible wages wouldn't become our mortgage guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your partner stopped wanting the larger house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we wouldn't resume the search under this plan. The agreement is continuing, not permission I've stored up for a later purchase. My tools can stay in the present house until my partner and I agree a move and the figures fit.

say: I'd use **ten years** for wanted choices as well as risk checks, without directing the children into my trade.
I'd keep **earning** while admitting the later dates do not guarantee retirement or an unchanged job.
think: Current **wages and reserve** make the next few years secure while later jobs and family needs remain uncertain.
I can't assume **pension access** or adult children's wages settle the mortgage at either later technology date.
do: Keep the **present house** for a year only with partner agreement, then review actual prices and wages.
Resume searching only with **continuing consent**, reserve untouched and written wages covering moving fees, new housing and travel.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 and repeat the household cost check before any housing commitment.
feel: **Calm** about near-term finances, with space to enjoy family life while keeping later commitments conditional.
S4.quote: My tools can stay in the present house until my partner and I agree a move and the figures fit.
fieldNote: He ages **both children** before considering later support needs, counting neither their wages nor an assumed pension as purchase money.
The **longer warning** permits an earlier review without relaxing continuing consent, reserve protection or complete costs before a commitment.

steps.text: Keep present house a year with partner agreement; restart search only with consent and reserve untouched
Resume only when written wages cover all moving fees, new housing and travel costs
Keep actual paid repairs after 2036 and repeat the household check before any housing commitment

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could reduce both physical repair incomes before we'd had as much time to adjust. Clear paid hours and real costs for any new work arrangement would help. I'd want room to check a useful idea without calling my family reserve the price of being modern.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how much of somebody's ambitious plan is a family need and how much is a wanted toy. My master electrician's licence doesn't make a bigger workshop a household necessity. I'd rather admit the want and check it than call every wish preparation.

headlineQuote: My master electrician's licence doesn't make a bigger workshop a household necessity.
portrait: **Erik, 43**, is a highly skilled lead with a two-year technical diploma, master electrician's licence and higher trade pay.
His **partner repairs upholstery**, with two school-age children, a mortgage, fifteen months saved and plenty of local electrical employers.
He uses **AI daily**, proposing invoice automation only with employer approval, paid setup, unchanged wages and human authorisation before customer use.
His **larger-house plan** depends on continuing partner consent, reserve protection and written wages covering moving fees, housing and travel before commitment.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives less preparation time before robots around 2031 could affect both adults' physical repair incomes.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **paid hours** and real costs would help compare actual work arrangements.
Room for **checked experiments** would support useful change without treating the family reserve as business spending.
